title: Why Warm Weather May Have Saved the Crocodiles
summary: Sixty-six million years ago, an asteroid strike wiped out the dinosaurs. So why did crocodiles survive? New research points to a simple habit: crocodiles and their ancient relatives loved warm weather, and that love may have saved them. Scientists led by University College London, known as UCL, studied more than 7,000 fossils and records from over 400 living and extinct species. They combined that evidence with computer models that rebuilt Earth's climate and geography across 245 million years. Their study was published in Science Advances. The team found a clear pattern. For much of their 250-million-year history, crocodile relatives followed warm climates. When Earth grew hotter, they expanded into new regions, sometimes reaching as far as Antarctica. When temperatures fell, they moved back toward the tropics. That pattern mattered after the asteroid struck. The simulations suggested that tropical and subtropical regions stayed suitable for crocodile relatives, even as conditions for many dinosaurs got worse. Areas near the equator could have stayed warm enough to shelter surviving populations, which later recovered and spread out again. Only the most extreme climate simulations removed these refuges. Earlier work by members of the same team found that suitable habitats for non-avian dinosaurs, the dinosaurs that went extinct, shrank much more severely. Lead author Dr. Alfio Alessandro Chiarenza, based at UCL Earth Sciences, explained it this way: the asteroid did not make the whole planet equally hostile to every group. Crocodiles' long-standing preference for warm places may have put survivors exactly where suitable climates held up best. Their history was also far more varied than today's crocodiles suggest. The wider group, called pseudosuchians, included heavily armored plant eaters, land hunters, and giants weighing more than a metric ton, including Sarcosuchus, the 12-meter 'super croc.'
why_it_matters: It shows that surviving a mass extinction can depend on being in places where suitable climates hold up, not only on surviving the disaster itself, and it helps explain why some groups recovered and spread again while non-avian dinosaurs did not.

background_read: Crocodiles belong to a much wider ancient group called pseudosuchians, which included many different kinds of animals, from heavily armored plant eaters to land hunters and giant predators.
For most of their long history, these animals followed warm climates, spreading into new regions when Earth grew hotter and moving back toward the tropics when it grew cooler.
Warm tropical and subtropical regions could therefore act as refuges where conditions stayed suitable, even when conditions elsewhere became much harder for other animals.
That long-standing preference for warm places may help explain why crocodile relatives survived a major extinction event that wiped out many dinosaurs.
